analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above roughly $50 million at annual rates from 2 to 8 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 2025 and has had no action since, with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new annual tax on total wealth — not income — for the country's richest households. A household's net worth above a threshold of at least $50 million would be taxed at 2%, rising to 8% on wealth above roughly $50 billion. It includes detailed rules for valuing hard-to-price assets like private businesses, requires the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax filers each year, and lets taxpayers who are asset-rich but cash-poor delay payment for up to five years. Nobody with wealth below the threshold would owe anything.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers whose net worth falls below the threshold — everyone below roughly $50 million — would owe nothing, while the tax would fall entirely on the top slice of households and trusts. To the extent the revenue or reduced wealth concentration funds government or lowers other tax burdens, the broad public benefits. The bill does not earmark the money for any specific use.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only to wealth above a threshold set at 1,000 times the greater of $50,000 or median U.S. household wealth, so at minimum only households above $50 million in net worth pay, and the threshold rises automatically if median household wealth grows.

Rates are tiered by wealth: 2% on the first band above the threshold, 4% above ten times the threshold, 6% above one hundred times, and 8% on wealth above one thousand times the threshold, with trusts taxed at a flat 8% above the threshold.

Everyday assets are excluded: tangible personal property worth $50,000 or less (other than collectibles, vehicles, boats, and aircraft) is not counted, so no ordinary family's home contents, tools, or savings are swept in.

The bill includes anti-avoidance measures: grantor and beneficiary trusts are attributed to the people behind them, gifts to children under 18 are counted as the giver's property, expatriates are taxed on the eve of leaving, and the IRS must audit at least 30% of wealth-tax filers every year.

Taxpayers facing severe liquidity constraints or hardship to an ongoing business can defer payment for up to five years, and owners of hard-to-value private assets get valuation rules established by the Treasury.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and trusts with net worth above the threshold — at least $50 million — would pay an annual tax of 2% to 8% on the excess, with married couples treated as a single taxpayer and the tax not deductible from income taxes. Wealthy families would also face new reporting requirements and penalties of 30% to 50% for large valuation understatements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and trusts worth over $50 million

drawbacks.text: Valuing private businesses, art, and other non-traded assets is genuinely hard, and the bill asks Treasury to build formulaic and retrospective valuation methods that don't currently exist, creating a real risk of disputes, litigation, and inconsistent assessments for owners of private companies.

Owners of asset-rich but cash-poor businesses — a family farm or an operating company worth over the threshold — could face a tax bill each year on wealth they have not sold, and while the bill allows up to a five-year payment deferral, that defers rather than eliminates the problem.

An annual tax on wealth held in any form, wherever situated, raises constitutional and administrative questions that courts would likely have to resolve, since the tax reaches non-traded property and worldwide assets; the bill addresses some avoidance channels but cannot guarantee none remain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it worked as designed, the bill would shift a meaningful share of federal taxation onto households above $50 million in net worth while leaving everyone else untouched, which is a substantial benefit to the broad public. The honest costs are administrative: valuing illiquid wealth annually is difficult and contestable, and asset-rich, cash-poor families with businesses or farms above the threshold would face real payment pressure even with the deferral option. The bill is unusually detailed about enforcement and anti-avoidance, which suggests the drafters took those problems seriously, but no wealth tax of this scope has been implemented in the U.S.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it has sat without a hearing or vote since April 2025 while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Summer Lee of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on April 14, 2025, joined by ten original cosponsors including Reps. Tlaib, Nadler, Frost, Norton, Dean, Ramirez, Huffman, Foushee, and Watson Coleman.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
The bill now has 12 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral to committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The households and trusts that would have owed the new tax are better off because the bill has gone nowhere; the current tax treatment of large fortunes is unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy households that would have paid the tax

for.name: Rep. Summer Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 12 Democratic cosponsors for a 2-8% annual wealth tax on fortunes above roughly $50 million.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Jerry Nadler, Rep. Maxwell Frost, and 9 other House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing total support to 12 members, all Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 14, 2025 and has taken no action since — no hearing, no markup, no vote reported from the action history.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority, which has not acted on it.

industries.industry: Ultra-wealthy households and trusts (net worth above $50 million)
industries.note: They would owe an annual tax of 2-8% on wealth above the threshold, on top of existing income and estate taxes, with no deduction from income taxes allowed. This is the bill's entire point: the cost lands on them and the benefit to everyone else is whatever the revenue and reduced concentration produce.

industries.industry: Wealth management, estate planning, and trust services
industries.note: An annual tax on net wealth with trust-attribution rules and gift rules would sharply reduce demand for the structures this industry sells to park and pass along large fortunes tax-efficiently.

industries.industry: Owners of large private businesses and family firms
industries.note: Owners whose stakes push net worth over the threshold would face annual bills on unsold assets, softened by a five-year deferral for liquidity hardship and by Treasury-set valuation methods for hard-to-price assets.

They would take on new information-reporting duties on clients' asset values, and could face penalties for large valuation understatements, but compliance work on behalf of wealthy clients is also billable business.

analysis.trajectory: A first-session bill with 12 cosponsors, all from the minority party, referred to the tax-writing committee, has essentially no path forward. Ways and Means tax bills originate with the chair and majority; a minority-sponsored wealth tax would need a hearing and markup that the majority shows no sign of scheduling. Expect it to sit in committee and expire when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless it is folded into a larger tax package, which would require majority support it does not currently have.
